title: Student Grants
subtitle: Build the school-year funding stack before accepting the loan balance

blocks.text: Tuition is one number. School somehow adds books, bus fare, groceries and a laptop charger that disappears precisely during midterms.

Canada Student Grants are student aid you do not pay back. You apply through the province or territory where you live for good. One application usually checks you for both grants and loans, federal and provincial. The amount depends on your need, your course load, your program and school, your family income and things like having children or a disability.
This lesson follows the money through a whole school year: what each dollar is, what the year really costs, where the deposit should go when it lands, and what happens after the last exam.
For the 2026–27 school year, the Canada Student Grant for Full-Time Students pays up to $4,200 a year, or $525 for each month of study. “Up to” depends on your need and income.

blocks.text: Canada: Student grants and loans
Knowing which school money you never pay back lets you borrow less and finish with a smaller debt.
blocks.detail: Four kinds of money can land in the same account, and only one expects to be repaid on its own terms.
blocks.extra: Section 02 helps you label every dollar.

sections.title: Give Every Dollar the Right Label

blocks.text: Four kinds of money can land in the same account. Only one of them expects to be repaid on its own terms.

items.title: GRANT
items.text: Usually not paid back if you still qualify and stay enrolled. Getting too much, or a change in your status, can still mean paying some back.

items.title: LOAN
items.text: Borrowed student aid that you must pay back. Federal Canada Student Loans have no interest, but you still have to repay them, and the provincial part has its own rules.

items.title: SCHOLARSHIP OR BURSARY
items.text: Money from your school, community, employer or a private group, with its own rules about grades, need, reports and renewal.

items.title: WORK AND SAVINGS
items.text: Job income, RESP withdrawals, family help and savings can change your budget and sometimes your aid. Declare what the application asks for.

blocks.text: For 2026–27, the part-time student grant is up to $2,520 a year and cannot be more than your assessed need. Part-time status follows student aid rules, not your opinion of a busy Tuesday.

items.title: “A grant can never be converted into money owing.”
items.text: Dropping out, a change in course load, not confirming you are enrolled or a new review can turn part of a grant into a loan or an overpayment. “Not paid back” assumes your file stays accurate.

blocks.text: The Northwest Territories, Nunavut and Quebec run their own student aid systems instead of Canada Student Grants and Loans. Apply through the right one.
Canada: Apply through your province

sections.title: Price the Whole Year Before You Accept a Loan

blocks.text: Student aid works out your need from a standard list of costs. Your real year may cost more or less. Build your own budget first, so you know how much of the loan offer you actually need. You can usually accept less than the full loan.
Here is an example of an eight-month college year for a student who rents a room. Swap in your own numbers.
$18,400 for the year − $4,200 grant − $3,000 from work and savings = $11,200 left to cover.
blocks.extra: Only that $11,200 needs a loan. Borrowing the full offer just because it was offered is optional.

items.title: Cost of the school year
items.text: Does this match what you will really spend, not the school’s brochure?

items.title: Tuition and fees
items.text: When is it due, and does aid pay it straight to the school?

items.title: Rent for eight months
items.text: Are you paying for a lease that runs longer than the school year?

items.title: Groceries
items.text: Is a meal plan cheaper or more expensive than cooking?

items.title: Books and supplies
items.text: Can you buy used, borrow from the library or wait for the syllabus?

items.title: Bus pass
items.text: Does your school fee already include a transit pass?

items.title: Phone and personal costs
items.text: What small monthly bills will follow you to school?

blocks.text: Aid usually arrives in parts, often once per term. Tuition may be paid to the school first, so only the rest reaches your bank. When it lands, give each dollar a job before the term starts, or the first month will spend the second month’s rent.
Give your aid deposit a job
blocks.extra: Enter the aid for the term and the tuition your school took first. Give every dollar that reaches you a job until nothing is left unassigned.

items.title: “If the loan offer is bigger than I need, I should take it all just in case.”
items.text: You can usually accept a smaller amount, and you can ask for more later if your costs change. Every extra dollar borrowed is a dollar you repay after graduation.

sections.title: One Application Can Ask About Several Grants

blocks.text: Students with children, students with disabilities and part-time students may get extra help. Fill in the right part of the application and send the papers it asks for. Do not assume the basic grant covers everything.

items.title: HELP FOR EACH CHILD OR DEPENDANT
items.text: Full-time students who qualify may get up to $2,240 a year for each dependant, on top of the full-time grant.

items.title: STUDENTS WITH DISABILITIES
items.text: The Canada Student Grant for Students with Disabilities is $2,800 a year. You need proof of your disability, such as a doctor’s form or a past assessment.

items.title: SERVICES AND EQUIPMENT
items.text: A separate grant can pay for approved costs like tutors, note-takers or assistive technology, up to $20,000 a school year.

blocks.text: After you are assessed, compare the total aid with your real budget for the school year. Money may come in parts after your school confirms you are enrolled. Do not spend a grant twice just because the provincial site and NSLSC both show it.

items.title: “The assessment amount is guaranteed until graduation.”
items.text: Aid is reviewed every school year and can change with your income, program, course load, family or policy. Reapply and update your file each year.

sections.title: Mina and the Grant That Appeared Twice

blocks.text: Meet Mina
paragraphs: Mina Tran starts nursing school in Winnipeg. Her goal is to finish without a pile of debt, so she plans her eight months down to the dollar: rent, food, the bus and her hospital placements.

She logs in to her provincial student aid account and sees a federal grant and a loan. Then she logs in to NSLSC and sees the same kind of money again. Mina briefly believes the grant has duplicated itself out of academic enthusiasm.
She is tempted to plan around both totals. There is a used laptop she needs, and a deposit for a better room near the hospital. With double the money, she could say yes to both.
Before she spends a dollar, Mina decides to check the money in three places: her award letter, her school account and her bank. It takes one evening and a lot of tea.
The truth is simple. Both screens show the same award. Tuition goes straight to the school first, and only the rest reaches her bank. Her budget had counted every number it saw as new money.
There is one good surprise. Her application asked about disability, and she had skipped it. She sends the papers in, and a disability grant covers the laptop.
Her funding does not shrink. Her double-counting does. Mina ends up with one grant, one loan, one laptop and one budget that knows the difference.

items.title: AWARD LETTER
items.text: One grant, one loan

items.title: SCHOOL ACCOUNT
items.text: Tuition paid first

items.title: BANK
items.text: Only the rest arrives

blocks.text: What resolved the conflict?
One award can show up on two screens without doubling. Match the letter, school account and deposit before you budget a single dollar twice.
Mina avoided spending her grant twice, and found a disability grant she had missed, by checking three places.
blocks.detail: Matching your award letter, school account and bank deposit can protect your own budget all year.
blocks.extra: Section 06 shows what happens to the loan after the last exam.

sections.title: After the Last Exam: Repayment Has a Safety Net

blocks.text: Federal Canada Student Loans no longer charge interest, but they still have to be repaid. Repayment usually starts six months after you leave school or drop below the course load for your aid. The provincial part of your loan may have its own interest and rules, so check both.
Four numbers to know before you graduate

items.title: Grace before payments
items.text: 6 months — after you leave school, before your first loan payment is due.

items.title: Low income
items.text: $0 a month — under the Repayment Assistance Plan when your income is below its threshold.

items.title: Stay on the plan
items.text: Twice a year — you reapply, every six months, to keep repayment help.

items.title: Lifetime limit
items.text: 340 weeks — of full-time aid for most students. Doctoral students and students with disabilities have different limits.

blocks.text: The Repayment Assistance Plan, or RAP, sets your federal payment based on your family income and size, not your loan balance. The zero-payment level for a single person was raised to $40,000 and now rises with inflation each year. Apply through the National Student Loans Service Centre. Your province may have a similar plan for its part of the loan.
If a payment looks impossible, ask for repayment help before you miss it. A loan left unpaid can go to collections and hurt your credit for years, even though help was free to ask for.

items.title: “If I cannot pay, ignoring the loan is the safest thing to do.”
items.text: Ignoring it is the expensive choice. Repayment help, a payment pause or a lower payment are all easier to get while your account is in good standing.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: Why is one student-aid application often enough?
items.detail: Most students send one provincial or territorial student aid application and are checked for federal and local aid in it.

items.title: How is a grant different from a loan?
items.detail: A grant is usually not paid back if you still qualify and stay enrolled. A loan is borrowed aid that you must pay back.

items.title: Your year costs $16,000. You have a $4,200 grant and $2,500 from work. How much do you need to borrow?
items.detail: $9,300. That is $16,000 − $4,200 − $2,500. You can usually accept less than the full loan offer.

items.title: Aid of $8,000 arrives, and $3,000 of tuition was paid to the school first. How much needs a job in your budget?
items.detail: $5,000. Give it to rent, books, food, transit and a small cushion before the term starts.

items.title: Which places run their own student aid instead of Canada Student Grants and Loans?
items.detail: The Northwest Territories, Nunavut and Quebec.

items.title: When do federal student loan payments usually start?
items.detail: Six months after you leave school. The Repayment Assistance Plan can lower the payment, even to $0, if your income is low.

items.title: What changes can lead to a review or an overpayment?
items.detail: Dropping out, a change in course load, not confirming you are enrolled or a new review can turn part of an award into a loan or overpayment.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): School-Year Funding Stack and Gap Plan

blocks.text: Use rounded numbers and short labels. Do not write student numbers, bank details or logins here.
Check your provincial account and NSLSC after each term starts. Confirming your enrolment late can hold up money you already qualified for.
Borrow the gap, not the offer.
blocks.detail: Apply early through the right province or territory, tell them about everything that applies, price your real year, give every deposit a job and ask for repayment help before you need it.

items.title: Assessed need
items.text: Your school costs minus the money you are expected to have, under aid rules.

items.title: Grant
items.text: Student aid you usually do not pay back if you keep meeting the rules.

items.title: Student loan
items.text: Borrowed aid that you must pay back.

items.title: Study period
items.text: The dates used to work out your costs and aid.

items.title: Enrolment confirmation
items.text: Your school’s proof that you are enrolled, which releases your funds.

items.title: Disbursement
items.text: One payment of your aid, often made once per term.

items.title: Overaward
items.text: Aid above what you now qualify for, which you may have to pay back.

items.title: Grace period
items.text: The six months after school before federal loan payments start.

items.title: RAP
items.text: Repayment Assistance Plan. Lowers your federal loan payment based on income and family size.

items.title: NSLSC
items.text: National Student Loans Service Centre.
